en: Parted from the great ones,
I wandered in misery and confusion—
Was this how you wished me to die?
I burned and baked, becoming an ember;
I was shattered and came to nothing.
I was a fine steed, but I wasted away;
I was a blue-maned lion, but I grew weary.
I burned away and lost
Half the youth of the blue-maned lion.
Steel softened and I became brass;
I faced many a storm,
And was gnawed and devoured by nobles.
They called me gray-bearded Bakai,
And I became a byword among cruel foes.
My wings, my pinions, and my tail
Were plucked, trimmed, and devoured.
My brain boiled where no water could reach,
And I became a barren desert where no grass grows.
Stripped of tail and mane,
I became the wild ass of that desert.
Neither dying nor vanishing, I grieved;
O bloodthirsty lion whom I cherished,
O leopard, I was parted from you.
My eyes became blood-filled sores;
I became a soul no longer needed.
I was once a proud and splendid man,
But became a stooping old man.
My waist was bent like a fox’s;
My vigor gone, my wretched soul
I burdened upon the beasts of night.
From my earliest days, I, Bakai,
Was born to be a warrior;
But when the hero vanished from sight,
I was beset by so many calamities.
My wretched soul was dragged
Like a kökbörü carcass among strongmen.
Our years stretched long in mockery.
The hero’s son Seytek.
To see his father’s face,
His fitting words came too late,
His two eyes strained into four,
Burning, seething, surging,
To his father, the bloodthirsty prince,
Noble Seytek pleaded.
If he wished his people well,
Seytek, who had remained behind,
Looked upon Semetey:
His beard was like an arrow case,
And when he looked at his mustache,
It was like the blade of an ornate sheath.
The breath that issued from his mouth
Was like a flame that ravaged a valley.
His lashes were flame, his eyes were embers;
No man possessed such fearful power.
His ferocity and lionheartedness
Surpassed the whole wide world.
My father the khan’s valor—
His face was dark, his speech fierce,
His courage unmatched, his wrath ablaze.
My leopard father was like a lion;
There is no such mortal in the world.
His round ears were like shields,
His great eyes like the Morning Star,
His aquiline nose like a mountain ridge,
The breath that issued from his mouth
Was like the wind through a palace gorge.
Whoever roused his anger,
He seemed able to devour with all his age.
Of middle height and broad of shoulder,
He bristled with boundless valor,
Like a black-mottled leopard
Rearing up beside him.
Like a short-maned gray lion
About to tear open a wound,
He made ready on every side.
A towering black camel of singular form
Pressed forward behind him.
The blessed child you bore in your womb—
You have subjected him to every trial;
The wife lovely as the promised moon,
The wise one cherished by all,
You have left a widow all these years.
Your chosen mount is the black-bay steed;
Behind you the black-faced woman laments.
From this moment take the grief-stricken woman
And bear her away at your saddle bow.
May fortune favor this fleeting world,
So we may share the ordained burden,
So we may meet and lie together,
So we may melt and know each other’s secrets,
So we may unite and journey together.
Take your poor wretch with you;
Keep me ruling in your heart,
Though you travel far on many journeys.
Gray-maned prince and leopard,
Bear me away at your saddle bow.
All my many kinds of dresses,
Though I heap them up, will not reach my neck;
Do not leave this hapless head in want,
But take me into your embrace.”
So saying, she wailed aloud,
And Aichürök sobbed and wept;
Every living soul melted,
All the sorrowful met that day,
All the dear ones sobbed,
And all who remained cried out.
The ancient cavern and the curved cliffs seemed to melt,
As parents and child were reunited.
The Black Giant and Külchoro,
And all the warriors, grew excited;
All those burdened by sorrow
Met the hero upon the open plain,
And stood there overwhelmed.
Before he had finished speaking,
The people’s thoughts were divided;
See what such a parting was like—
He had gone and encountered,
Chasing the white doe,
And truly had turned her into a cow.
My lion father had indeed
Brought the whole world under his command.
My gray-maned father stirred up strife,
Chased the gray doe and turned her into a cow,
And wherever he appeared, imposed his will.
He shattered the Chinese and opened a road,
Struck down the reluctant and seized booty,
Attacked mighty nations,
Scoured the passes and captured the heights,
And, splendidly arrayed, took many ridges.
He became a banner to his kinsmen;
When he faced a watchful foe,
He became a blazing conflagration.
He was the fortress of the Ala-Too;
Of my poor gray-maned father,
The spiteful enemy who plotted against him
Would ask, “From where did he arise?”
Whoever remembered him was amazed;
He was the people’s great champion.
He slipped an arrow from his quiver,
And whoever came out to exchange shots
With my peerless lion father was crushed.
None who challenged him survived.
His weapons numbered eighty-four,
His stroke was a crimson fire;
None who faced him remained alive.
Whoever confronted him fled like the wind;
Whoever exchanged shots with him was ruined.
The enemies who beheld his majesty
Despaired of their borrowed lives.
When dust spread across the wide plain,
It became the ground for bitter combat.
My devastating gray-maned father
Settled in the heart of Talas
And tethered his fourteen steeds.
Enemies who came out shooting
He drove before him.
When they provoked his anger,
From six ravines he hauled up
Sixty pairs of black camels.
A fearsome tiger was his guardian;
Broad-chested, himself a lion,
No living soul could equal him.
No mortal could approach him head-on,
No enemy could prevail against him;
He readied himself like a tiger,
And none he charged survived.
His supreme courage was like a mountain ridge;
My lion father beyond all reckoning
Seemed able to devour a man in wrestling.
His silhouette was like a fortress,
As though it would swallow any attacker.
His beard was like a grove of plane trees;
When he descended, all seemed shattered—
So exceedingly was he made.”
Thus the warrior Seytek reflected,
His father appearing before his eyes,
His mind bewildered and divided,
And now he stood content.
His first forefather was Tügöl Khan;
Kara Khan never leaves his descendants.
The sharp steel sword truly has a sheath.
The people clamored and raised a tumult,
The nation went about in uproar—
It was no lie but the truth.
May God never take away a father;
May no child be left behind
Without knowing his father alive.
If the Creator is indeed true,
May He never inflict such humiliation
Upon one of His servants.
My heart was troubled with grief;
This time my eyes have seen
My gray-maned lion father,
So I bear no grievance against God.
He is both bloodthirsty and lionhearted;
All twelve limbs of my dear
Gray-maned father are whole.
See how he burns and cries out.
Father and son have met;
See how they surge with emotion.
To embrace each other once,
Making heaven and earth resound,
To greet each other just once—
See how they burn with longing.
The hero Semetey
Had no words to speak,
No eyes with which to gaze,
No potent medicine to restore him;
Such filth is this world.
The generous lion, led astray,
Met his own son,
Yet stood there without recognizing him.
Semetey then spoke these words,
Telling of horrors before their meeting:
“Born of a mother, I became a lion;
I brought the whole world beneath my rule,
And became a gray-maned lion of a man.
Led astray by the enemy,
I became one who fled his people.
I took a cavern for my home;
I turned back after my people were scattered,
And was separated from Külchoro,
Who had sat there as my protector.
I scouted the land and grieved;
I was parted from mother, child, and wife,
From my Kyrgyz people with their cities,
And from all those who remained.
A person longs for one to ride;
She lured me and bound me.
Kökmonchok, daughter of the peri,
Aichürök’s younger sister,
Grew up and blocked my road,
Bewitched me and bound my hands,
And showed me many wonders.
I am not dead but alive,
One of those who have not died.
She bound my eyes so I could not see,
And chewed me between her teeth.
Those she stabbed were countless and turned to ash;
Her army numbered tens of thousands.
The steel city was a great fortress;
By my reckoning, my father was mighty.
Defeated by the Jediger,
Why was my noble father, that dear lion,
Reduced to such humiliation?
He filled and dammed the broad yellow valley,
Growing stronger each time he died,
Smoldering anew whenever he was spent,
And gaining strength from his very roots.
Each time he died, he flourished;
He was both sovereign and lionhearted.
My oceanic, gray-maned lion father
Was blessed with perfect fortune;
Indeed, my father was so great a hero.
That I was made Semetey’s son
Leaves me no grievance against God.
